1.d4 e5.name: Englund Gambit
1.d4 e5.background: Named after the Swedish player Fritz Englund (1871–1933), who sponsored a thematic tournament in 1932–33 in which every game began with the position after 4.Qd5. Kārlis Bētiņš (1867–1943) introduced the main line with 2...Nc6 and 3...Qe7, and Henry Charlick, the second Australian champion, introduced the 2...d6 line in the early 1890s.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn, the sound answer to a gambit that offers it for no concrete return: White is a pawn up and Black must prove his compensation. White's task is calm development while avoiding traps against loose pieces and pawns; the extra pawn is the long-term trump.

1.d4 e5 2.d5.name: Englund Gambit Declined
1.d4 e5 2.d5.strategy: Declines by closing the centre: the e5 pawn is safe from capture, but White passes up the free pawn and the chance to punish the gambit. Black develops freely and gets an easy, equal game.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3.name: Englund Gambit Declined: Reversed Alekhine
1.d4 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops and protects d4, but lets Black push the pawn forward with gain of time: it attacks the knight and takes space. White avoids the gambit but is a move behind in the fight for the centre.

1.d4 e5 2.e3.name: Englund Gambit Declined: Reversed French
1.d4 e5 2.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, but declines the pawn: Black can trade on d4 and reach a balanced, open game with the gambit gone. White passes up the chance to punish 1...e5 for a quiet game of equal chances.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to an active diagonal at once, aimed at f2. With the centre closed Black has given no pawn and White has taken none, so Black gets a healthy game; White's space gain is not backed by development.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d5 and discourages e4, which Black can answer by taking the pawn. Black keeps the e-pawn and gets a healthy game, since White has gained space but no development.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 d6.strategy: Supports the e5 pawn and frees the c8-bishop, accepting a closed centre. It is safe, but passive: Black has not used the chance to develop with tempo, and White gets time to build behind its space advantage.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.e4.strategy: Takes the centre and space at once. The queen sortie ...Qh4 hits e4 and f2 together, but Qf3 covers both and the game stays level. White commits to a broad centre that Black's bishop and queen will harass.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight with an attack on the e5 pawn, which the bishop does not guard, and covers h4, so the queen sortie that punishes e4 never comes. White keeps the space gained and makes Black react to the threat.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.e3.strategy: Shuts the bishop's diagonal at once, so f2 is no longer a target and no queen sortie hurts. A solid answer to the bishop's idea, at the price of blocking White's own queen's bishop for the moment.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.e4 Qh4.name: Englund Gambit Declined: Diemer Counterattack
1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.e4 Qh4.strategy: Springs the point of the bishop's sortie: the queen attacks e4 and, together with the bishop, f2, where mate is threatened. White has to defend at once, and Black takes the initiative with active pieces.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and attacks the e4 pawn, which nothing defends and which cannot advance past the e5 pawn. White has to defend it with a developing move, and Black keeps a healthy game; the queen sortie is the more forcing choice.

1.d4 e5 2.d5 Bc5 3.e4 d6.strategy: Supports the e5 pawn and keeps the structure solid, but is slow: it makes no threat, so White gets time to consolidate the space it has gained and can answer ...Qh4 with Nf3.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the e5 pawn at once, aiming to win it back through pressure and quick development rather than by offering more material. Black accepts a pawn deficit for activity while White has to defend a pawn far from his other pieces.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 d6.name: Englund Gambit: Hartlaub-Charlick Gambit
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 d6.background: Claude Bloodgood published a book on the gambit in 1998, Blackburne-Hartlaub Gambit, presenting theory he compiled during his prison sentence.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 d6.strategy: Offers a second pawn: after White takes on d6, Black recaptures with the bishop and gets open lines and quick development at the cost of material. White should stay ahead with careful, unhurried play but must watch for attacking tricks.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 f6.name: Englund Gambit: Soller Gambit
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 f6.strategy: Attacks e5 with a pawn to open lines and develop with tempo for the pawn given. The move weakens the kingside, and White can answer by ignoring the offer and building a strong centre, keeping a clear edge.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Qh4.name: Englund Gambit: Mosquito Gambit
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Qh4.strategy: Brings the queen out at once, eyeing f2, but nothing supports it: White chases it with a developing move such as Nf3 or g3 and keeps the extra pawn. Black has lost time as well as a pawn.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends the pawn with a developing move, the simplest way to keep the extra material. The knight is ideally placed on f3, and White can finish development in peace; the only challenge is to see the tactical tricks Black's quick development sets.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Bf4.strategy: Holds the extra pawn with a developing bishop, but ...g5 challenges it at once and the bishop must retreat while Black gains space. White stays ahead, though with less than after the knight move.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a knight but leaves e5 undefended, so Black takes the pawn back with ...Nxe5 at once. The extra pawn that made 2.dxe5 worthwhile is gone, and Black has recovered it with a developing move.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7.name: Englund Gambit: Main Line
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7.background: Henri Grob frequently used this version of the gambit, with 3...Qe7.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7.strategy: Adds a second attacker to e5, so Black threatens to win the pawn back, and prepares ...Qb4+ against careless development. The queen comes out early and blocks its own bishop, and White can meet the threat with a developing move.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 f6.name: Englund Gambit: Soller Gambit Deferred
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 f6.background: The gambit is named after Karl Soller. Detailed analysis in print has been limited to two German-language works by Stefan Bücker from the 1980s and 1990s, and in recent years International Master Kamran Shirazi has played it more than 1,400 times in online blitz and bullet games.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 f6.strategy: Challenges e5 with a pawn to open lines for the pieces and gets some play for it, but weakens the king's diagonal. White keeps a small edge, either by holding the extra pawn or by giving it back for a lead in development.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Bc5.name: Englund Gambit: Felbecker Gambit
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop toward f2 and prepares a pawn lever against e5, but it does not touch e5 itself, so White keeps the pawn for now. Black bets on rapid development rather than direct recovery of the material.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Nge7.name: Englund Gambit: Zilbermints Gambit
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Nge7.background: The gambit is named after the American player Lev D. Zilbermints, who had extensive analysis of the line published in Blackmar Diemer Gambit World (issues 61–63). Stefan Bücker analysed it further in Kaissiber 5 and 6.
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Nge7.strategy: Intends to attack e5 a second time via g6, but needs two moves and blocks the f8-bishop, so White has time to defend or develop. A slow route to regain the pawn, relying on arriving before White consolidates.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 d6.strategy: Challenges e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, the least costly way to carry on the gambit. Black stays a pawn down, but nothing is weakened and development comes quickly, so White has to keep the extra pawn with care.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Qd5.name: Englund Gambit: Stockholm Variation
1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Qd5.strategy: Guards e5 from the centre to keep the pawn, but the queen is exposed: ...f6 challenges e5 at once and the queen soon has to move again with a gain of time for Black. White stays a pawn up, though with much less than a developing move keeps.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4.strategy: The main line: White defends e5 with a developing move and lets Black win the b2 pawn with the queen. That leaves material level but White ahead in development against a queen far from home, so White plays for the initiative rather than for the extra pawn.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops with the idea of giving the pawn back at once. Black recaptures on e5, but White gets a lead in development and a free hand in the centre against a queen that stands awkwardly on e7. White plays for an edge in activity rather than material.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.name: Englund Gambit Declined: Reversed Krebs
1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.strategy: Gains space and a tempo: the pawn hits the knight, which must move. Black takes more of the centre and cramps White's kingside development, accepting that the advanced pawn may become a target later.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 exd4.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens the centre. After the knight recaptures, Black can take a share of the centre with a pawn of its own and challenge the knight: a simple, sound route that avoids the weaknesses of an advanced pawn.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Offers the e5 pawn for a lead in development that does not materialise. White takes on e5, Black recaptures, and the knight takes the pawn in turn, so Black is simply a pawn down whether or not the queens come off.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4 3.Ng1.name: Englund Gambit Declined: Reversed Brooklyn
1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4 3.Ng1.strategy: Retreats to the starting square: the knight has lost two moves while Black's pawn has gained space on e4. White avoids complications but trails in development and space and lets Black play comfortably.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4 3.Ne5.name: Englund Gambit Declined: Reversed Mokele Mbembe
1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4 3.Ne5.strategy: Jumps into the centre, but ...d6 kicks the knight away again, so Black gains time and space while White gets no lasting outpost. White's pieces end up tied to repairing the damage.

1.d4 e5 2.Nf3 e4 3.Nfd2.strategy: The usual retreat: the knight steps back to a square from where it eyes the advanced pawn, which has no defender yet, so Black has to hold it. It blocks the c1-bishop for now, but White keeps a sound centre and trusts the pawn on e4 to become a target as Black spends moves protecting it.
